state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a favorite song playing on your phone. If you were to move three steps away from your phone, would the song change or would it just sound a bit quieter? Just like the song stays the same but becomes quieter as you move away, the function \( f(x-3) \) is still the same function \( f(x) \), but it's shifted three units to the right. So, the translation is actually by the vector \(\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 0\end{array}\right]\).

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so it moves to the right, not up! But I'm still a bit confused - why does the minus sign in f(x-3) make it go right instead of left? Shouldn't minus mean it goes backwards?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it like this: when you are reading a book and you see "x-3," it means you need to go three pages back, not forward. Similarly, in math, when you see "f(x-3)," it means you move three units to the right, not left. So the minus sign actually shifts the graph in the opposite direction of what you might expect, just like going back in a book.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, I think I get it a bit more now, but the book example is confusing me - going back pages sounds like it should go left, not right? Like, could you maybe show me with an actual example, like with numbers or a graph, so I can see why f(x-3) moves right instead of left?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides correct mathematical content but uses confusing analogies that don't engage the core misconception, simply tells the answer rather than prompting reasoning, and the student remains confused and explicitly requests a different approach by Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use real-world analogies (phone/song, reading a book), these analogies are poorly chosen and confusing—they don't accurately map to the mathematical concept, as evidenced by the student's increasing confusion about why the transformations work the way they do.
